'''Combinatorial physics''' or '''physical combinatorics''' is the area of interaction between [[physics]] and [[combinatorics]].

==Overview==
:"Combinatorial Physics is an emerging area which unites combinatorial and discrete mathematical techniques applied to theoretical physics, especially Quantum Theory."<ref>[http://www.ifj.edu.pl/conf/combphys/index.html 2007 International Conference on Combinatorial physics]</ref>
:"Physical combinatorics might be defined naively as combinatorics guided by ideas or insights from physics"<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=ItPQassTBwsC Physical Combinatorics], [[Masaki Kashiwara]], Tetsuji Miwa, Springer, 2000, {{ISBN|0-8176-4175-0}}</ref>

Combinatorics has always played an important role in [[quantum field theory]] and [[statistical physics]].<ref>{{cite book | author= David Ruelle | title=Statistical Mechanics, Rigorous Results |
publisher= World Scientific | year=1999 | isbn=978-981-02-3862-9 }}</ref> However, combinatorial physics only emerged as a specific field after a seminal work by [[Alain Connes]] and [[Dirk Kreimer]],<ref>A. Connes, D. Kreimer,
[https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9912092 Renormalization in quantum field theory and the Riemann-Hilbert problem I], Commun. Math. Phys. 210 (2000), 249-273</ref> showing that the [[renormalization]] of [[Feynman diagram]]s can be described by a [[Hopf algebra]].

Combinatorial physics can be characterized by the use of algebraic concepts to interpret and solve physical problems involving combinatorics. It gives rise to a particularly harmonious collaboration between mathematicians and physicists.

Among the significant physical results of combinatorial physics, we may mention the reinterpretation of renormalization as a [[Riemann–Hilbert problem]],<ref>A. Connes, D. Kreimer,
[https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0003188 Renormalization in quantum field theory and the Riemann-Hilbert problem II], Commun. Math. Phys. 216 (2001), 215-241</ref> the fact that the [[Slavnov–Taylor identities]] of [[Gauge theory|gauge theories]] generate a Hopf ideal,<ref>W. D. van Suijlekom, [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0610137 Renormalization of gauge fields: A Hopf algebra approach], Commun. Math. Phys. 276 (2007), 773-798</ref> the [[Field quantization|quantization of fields]]<ref>C. Brouder, B. Fauser, A. Frabetti, R. Oeckl, [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0311253 Quantum field theory and Hopf algebra cohomology], J. Phys. A: Math. Gen. 37 (2004), 5895-5927</ref> and [[String theory|strings]],<ref>T. Asakawa, M. Mori, S. Watamura, [https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.2203 Hopf Algebra Symmetry and String Theory], Prog. Theor. Phys. 120 (2008), 659-689</ref> and a completely algebraic description of the combinatorics of quantum field theory.<ref>C. Brouder, [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0611153 Quantum field theory meets Hopf algebra], ''[[Mathematische Nachrichten]]'' 282 (2009), 1664-1690</ref> An important example of applying combinatorics to physics is the enumeration of [[alternating sign matrix]] in the solution of [[ice-type model]]s. The corresponding ice-type model is the six vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions.
